shortDef: Someone responsible for how a product works for its users.
longDef: The scope varies more than any other title in the field: some UX designers run research and information architecture, others produce screens. What is consistent is responsibility for the experience of using the thing, rather than only its appearance. Read the job description rather than the title, and ask what the last three projects actually involved.
example: One posting means research, flows and prototypes; another means visual design in an existing design system.
misuse: UX and UI are not two halves of one job. UI is one discipline within a broader practice that includes research and structure.

shortDef: Someone focused on the visual and interactive surface of a product.
longDef: UI design covers layout, typography, colour, iconography, states and the components a product is built from, usually within a design system. It is a craft discipline requiring real depth in visual communication, not a decorative step after the thinking. In smaller teams the same person also does the UX work, which is where the titles blur.
example: Defining every state of a form field, checking contrast in both themes, and adding it to the component library.
misuse: "Just make it pretty" misunderstands the role: hierarchy, contrast and state design are usability work.

shortDef: A designer accountable for outcomes, not just screens.
longDef: The title usually signals involvement from problem definition through to measurement: research, interaction, interface and the business case around them. It became common as companies wanted designers who could argue about what to build, not only how it should look. In practice it often means a UX designer expected to also engage with metrics and strategy.
example: Deciding with a PM that a feature should not be built, based on research, and proposing a smaller change instead.

shortDef: A designer specialising in behaviour: what happens when you act.
longDef: Interaction design concerns states, transitions, feedback, timing and the logic of a control — the parts of a design that only exist in motion or in response. It is the discipline behind gestures, complex components and anything with more than two states. It sits closest to engineering of the design specialisms.
example: Specifying what a card does on press, on long press, on drag, mid-flight, and when the network drops.

shortDef: Designing how interfaces move between states.
longDef: Motion in a product has jobs: showing where something came from, maintaining continuity, directing attention and confirming an action. Durations of roughly 150 to 350 milliseconds cover most interface transitions, with easing that starts fast and settles. Every motion decision needs a reduced-motion counterpart.
example: A sheet rising from the control that opened it, so the origin of the new surface is never in doubt.
misuse: Motion for delight alone becomes an obstacle by the hundredth time. Repeated interactions need the shortest motion that still reads.

shortDef: Someone who plans and runs studies to answer product questions.
longDef: Researchers choose methods, recruit appropriately, run studies without leading participants, and turn findings into decisions the team acts on. The hardest parts are usually choosing the right question and getting the results used, not running the sessions. In teams without a researcher, designers do this work with varying rigour.
example: Turning "is the new flow better?" into a benchmark comparing task success across two matched groups.

shortDef: Someone who designs and builds, usually in a design system.
longDef: They live between the two disciplines: prototyping in code, maintaining component libraries, and making sure what is designed can be built consistently. The role is most valuable where a design system exists, because that is where design decisions become code. It requires genuine competence in both, which is why the role is scarce.
example: Building the production Button component and its documentation from the design team's token definitions.

shortDef: Product, design and engineering leading a team together.
longDef: The three roles share responsibility for what gets built: desirability, viability and feasibility argued in the same room rather than passed between functions. It works when all three are involved from problem definition. It degrades into a relay when design joins after the decision has been made.
example: A PM, designer and tech lead jointly deciding to cut scope after a prototype test rather than escalating.

shortDef: Deep in one discipline, competent across several others.
longDef: The vertical stroke is your depth — the thing you are genuinely expert in — and the horizontal is enough breadth to collaborate credibly with adjacent disciplines. It describes what most product teams want: someone who can carry their own craft and speak engineering, research and content. Breadth without depth makes you replaceable; depth without breadth makes you hard to work with.
example: An interaction designer who can read a component's code, write clear microcopy and run a usability test.

shortDef: The documented expectations for each level of a role.
longDef: A ladder describes craft, scope, autonomy and influence at each level, and usually splits into individual contributor and management tracks past mid-level. Its value is making promotion criteria legible rather than political. Ladders that describe only craft tend to promote people into management as the only way to grow.
example: A senior level defined by leading a project end to end, a staff level by influencing several teams' direction.

shortDef: Someone accountable for a design team rather than for the designs.
longDef: The job is hiring, growing people, setting quality expectations, protecting focus and representing design outside the team. Craft judgement is still needed, but exercised through critique and standards rather than by doing the work. The common failure is a manager who keeps designing and leaves the team unmanaged.
example: Running weekly critique, setting the quality bar for accessibility, and negotiating research time with product leadership.

shortDef: How deeply design practice is embedded in an organisation.
longDef: Low maturity treats design as a service that styles decisions already made; high maturity involves design in framing problems and measures experience alongside commercial results. It shows in when designers are consulted, whether research budget exists, and whether accessibility is a requirement or a request. Knowing where an organisation sits is the most useful thing a candidate can establish in an interview.
example: Being asked to "make this screen nicer" a week before launch is a reliable indicator of low maturity.

shortDef: A curated set of work showing how you think, not just what you made.
longDef: Reviewers look for the problem, the constraints, what you decided and why, what you would do differently, and what actually happened. Three deep case studies beat twelve screenshots. Being explicit about your own contribution on team projects matters more than the polish of the final image.
example: A case study that opens with the business problem and the constraint, and closes with the measured result and a regret.
misuse: A gallery of finished screens with no reasoning is a gallery, not a portfolio.

shortDef: A written account of one project, from problem to outcome.
longDef: A strong case study states the problem and constraints, shows the options considered and why one was chosen, names the evidence, and reports what happened including what did not work. Length is not the point — a reviewer usually gives it a few minutes. Confidentiality can be handled by describing the reasoning without exposing the numbers.
example: "Support contacts about delivery fell by a fifth; the second change we shipped had no effect and we reverted it."
